entries.title: Trump Considers a Press Secretary Shakeup: Picking a Man
entries.summary: The president is considering a man to prevent comparisons with outgoing spokesperson Karoline Leavitt, sources say.
entries.content:
After four female press secretaries during his two terms, President Donald Trump has told close advisers he would prefer a man to fill Karoline Leavitt’s position, NOTUS has learned.

The pick would be meant to stave off comparisons with the outgoing press secretary, according to two sources familiar with the conversations. Leavitt plans to depart the White House at the end of the month.

Trump has signaled interest in Scott Jennings, a conservative media pundit who has been widely reported to be among those being considered for the position. Trump, however, is not quite sold on the idea, according to one source familiar with the conversations and granted anonymity to speak freely.

Other men have also been floated for the role, including Ari Fleischer, who served as press secretary under President George W. Bush.

Trump has mainly hired women to serve as his chief spokesperson.

Sean Spicer served for six months as Trump’s press secretary during his first term but was replaced by Sarah Huckabee Sanders who held the position until 2019. Stephanie Grisham and then Kayleigh McEnany held the role after Huckabee left. Leavitt has been Trump’s press secretary since the start of his second term.

The president has said he is in no rush to fill the position, according to one of those sources, and that instead the White House could adopt the same style of briefings that took place during Leavitt’s maternity leave from late April until returning in July.

During that time, Vice President JD Vance and multiple Cabinet members held press briefings, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

Last week, Leavitt announced she would step down at the end of August just a month after returning from maternity leave, citing the desire to spend time with her family. She plans to stay on as an outside senior adviser.

There’s also another option the president may consider.

A person close to the White House predicted that all of the attention on the president’s close aide Natalie Harp could catapult her into the position.

“She was on OANN,” the source said, referring to the One America News Network. The media, the person said, is going to “make her press secretary.”

entries.title: ‘Affordability’ Is This Year’s Buzzword. Just Not When Trump’s Talking.
entries.summary: As Americans struggle to afford the basics, the president keeps touting the hot economy and the need for a White House ballroom.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump spoke to a crowd of families in late July at a high school in Marietta, Georgia.

He talked about Venezuelan oil and the war in Iran. He ticked off investment commitments. And he touted provisions in the Republican tax bill — or tried to.

“This past filing season, 130,000 tipped workers right here in Georgia saved an average of more than $7,000 on their taxes. And that’s because of no tax on tips. You know, we’re building a tremendous military facility at the White House,” Trump said. “And they’ve been working hard, a lot of overtime.”

The speech in a state that will be pivotal in November was one of a handful Trump has delivered this year, part of what White House chief of staff Susie Wiles said in January would be weekly trips across the country to talk to voters ahead of the midterms.

Last month, the Pew Research Center asked voters what they most wanted to hear about from candidates. The answer was overwhelmingly cost of living, wages and affordability. More than half of voters think the economy is getting worse, according to a July Quinnipiac University poll. And 58% of those polled disapproved of Trump’s handling of the economy.

A March report found that nearly half of families do not make enough to cover the basic cost of living in their communities. Only 13% of Americans aged 18-29 believe the country is headed in the right direction, according to Harvard’s youth poll that was conducted last November.

But despite overwhelming evidence that affordability is defining the current political moment, the president is often reflexively dismissive of the issue.

“‘What are you going to do about the prices?’” Trump recounted in Georgia of a question he says he’s often asked. “They used a word — first time I heard it — it was a word made up by the Democrats: affordability. They said affordability.”

This is overwhelmingly the context in which Trump mentions affordability, a NOTUS review of Trump’s speaking events this year using Roll Call’s Factbase found. Republicans across the board say that Trump is instrumental to any win in November. But he rarely acknowledges the issue that will decide the election.

https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/seRx9/full.pngTrump’s mentions of key economic terms are rarely in the context of affordability. When the president uses the word “prices,” it is often to say that his administration inherited high prices and has worked to lower them.

“You know, and they have this term. So here I am, I’m one day in office and the fake news goes, ‘affordability, affordability.’ I said, ‘What’s that all about?’ ‘Prices are too high,’ I said, ‘I’m here for less than 24 hours,’” Trump told a crowd in Milford, Michigan, in July. “But we’ve brought down prices. Last week, it was announced that inflation has gone down faster than at any time in the last six years.”

A superlative almost always precedes Trump’s mentions of the economy — Trump frequently refers to the economy of his first term as “the greatest economy ever” and similarly praises his second-term economy.

“I proudly signed the largest tax cuts in American history for the second time, because in my first term, we had the greatest economy in the history of our country,” Trump said in Michigan. “Didn’t get credit, but that’s OK. But we had the greatest economy in the history of the country. And we’re blowing it away this time.”

While the economy may look broadly good on paper — the stock market is performing well and unemployment is low — Americans across the country are struggling with high housing costs, soaring grocery prices and wages that aren’t keeping up with inflation. For many households, the disconnect between economic indicators and their personal finances has continued to worsen.

Anne Hamming, the communications manager at Feeding America West Michigan, told NOTUS that her local branch of the hunger relief organization is seeing a higher rate of childhood food insecurity, which she said indicates that higher costs are squeezing families.

In lower-wage households, Hamming said, small increases in grocery costs or a trip to the gas station “make an impact.”

“They add up,” she said. “We hear all over the place that people are just really struggling.”

Bureau of Labor Statistics data released Wednesday paints this same picture in numbers: An increase in prices wiped out wage gains. Inflation and high energy prices, a result of the war in Iran, have added to the squeeze and worsened the cost-of-living problems plaguing many Americans.

In a statement to NOTUS, White House spokesperson Olivia Wales did not acknowledge NOTUS’ questions about the frequency of cost-of-living issues in the president’s statements.

“President Trump can walk and chew gum at the same time,” she said. “As a result, the Trump Administration continues to deliver on the President’s affordability agenda by lowering drug prices, reshoring American jobs, and cutting taxes while simultaneously touting a historic drop in violent crime nationwide and the most secure border in history.”

https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/Jyj7s/full.pngThe White House signaled an intention to focus on affordability and the midterms late last year.

“The president is very keyed into what’s going on, and he recognizes, like anybody, that it takes time to do an economic turnaround, but all the fundamentals are there, and I think you’ll see him be very, very focused on prices and cost of living,” former White House deputy chief of staff James Blair told Politico last November.

But for much of this year, other issues have captured a larger share of the president’s remarks — most notably the war in Iran and related foreign policy issues. The war is unpopular: A Politico poll conducted by Public First found that support for the war is slipping even among Trump’s most ardent supporters.

“With the economy, the biggest issue is two things. Number one, the discipline and consistency in talking about the wins that you’re having in the economy. The administration lacks a certain discipline that you get from mainstream administrations,” Cory Ruth, a Republican strategist, and industry consultancy company CEO in Georgia, told NOTUS. “The second thing is, there are people in his administration that are highly politicized, and the media is never going to take them at face value. And then there are people in the administration who the media does respect and does listen to. They’re less politicized, and he doesn’t do a good job of putting those people up front.”

The White House has undertaken efforts aimed at answering the affordability question. For example, it rolled out TrumpRx, a prescription drug website designed to offer deals on medication. But NOTUS found that Trump has only mentioned TrumpRx at eight speaking events since the platform launched in February.

While Congressional Republicans refer to last year’s tax bill as the “Working Families Tax Cuts Act,” Trump continues to call it the “Big, Beautiful Bill.” While he talks about its provisions like no tax on tips, which Republicans acknowledge are more popular than the legislation as a whole, he mentioned them in less than 20% of all transcribed speaking events this year.

“He ended taxes on overtime. If you are a sort of blue-collar worker or a working-class person, and you … are allowed to get overtime, that’s gone. And so there are things that he’s doing,” Ruth said, adding that the drumbeat of that messaging “is just not consistent enough.”

Before departing on a trip to China in May, Trump was asked whether he was taking into account Americans’ financial situations as he tried to negotiate an end to the Iran war.

“I don’t think about Americans’ financial situation, I don’t think about anybody,” Trump said. “I think about one thing. We can not let Iran have a nuclear weapon. That’s all. That’s the only thing that matters.”

Republicans previously told NOTUS that they were frustrated with that response, and with the way that he talks about the economy broadly. Democrats, on the other hand, said they have every intention of capitalizing on Trump’s perceived lack of concern.

“Americans’ financial situation is dire, and Republicans don’t think about anyone other than Donald Trump,” Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer said the next day.

Note: Sampled words may represent a combination of multiple terms. For example, “affordability” includes instances where the president said “afford,” “affordable,” and affordability. Others are as follows: costs (cost/costs/cost of living), wages (wage/wages/paycheck/pocket), economy (economy/economic), price (price/prices), and families (Family/families). 

Some statements were omitted based on context. For example, Trump saying on Feb. 20 that some Supreme Court justices were an “embarrassment to their families” was not included in the count for the term families, as families in that context is not related to affordability.

entries.title: Trump’s Allies Want to Know the Plan in Iran — If There Is One
entries.summary: Six months after starting a war and over 60 days after a deal that failed to end it, Trump’s allies want to know what the plan is to get out.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump’s shifting statements on Iran have made it difficult for even allies to know the real plan for the war — let alone defend it to the American people.

Two House members told NOTUS that they weren’t given talking points on the current status of the war by the White House before they left Washington for the August recess. A MAGA strategist who had been invited to private briefings about the war with Vice President JD Vance and other top officials said those meetings have ceased and information is scarce. And it’s been more than 100 days since the Department of Defense held a press briefing for reporters.

“I don't feel like I have good insight into their messaging strategy,” one person close to the Department of Defense said, requesting anonymity to speak freely. “I don't feel like I understand it actually at all.”

The lack of cohesive messaging has led some to conclude that there is no firm plan to end the conflict — which has now stretched on for six months — ahead of the midterm elections. Trump won’t be on the ballot, but the high prices that most Americans associate with the Iran war will be.

“For an ongoing war, there’s not all that much messaging around it,” a Republican strategist said, requesting anonymity to speak candidly.”And the messaging around it is just — it’s bungled, it’s bargled, it’s confused.”

Many of the president’s allies are eager for a conclusion to the war — but at a minimum, they want some clarity on what’s next. For some allies, it’s not clear what victory is supposed to look like.

“How do we finish the job? It has not been answered yet,” Republican Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota told NOTUS in an interview this month.

The administration has held over 30 bipartisan briefings with senior officials for Congress since the war began and during negotiations with Iran. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has typically led the briefings of Armed Services Committee members, according to multiple senators.

The White House objected to the idea that the path in Iran is unclear.

“President Trump has destroyed Iran’s military capabilities and is crushing what’s left of its abysmal economy with the most successful naval blockade in world history,” Olivia Wales, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement to NOTUS. “The President has been clear: He will always advance America’s interests and never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”

A memorandum of understanding meant to kick off the process of ending the war has expired. Just this week, the Trump administration has presented two very different pictures of the war.

Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law and a key negotiator with Iran, told Fox News on Monday that conversations with parts of the Iranian government were “more robust than it’s maybe ever been.”

The president contradicted him the next day.

“There are no talks or conversations going on, or scheduled, with the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump posted on Truth Social.

On Wednesday, when asked by NOTUS when he would restart negotiations with Iran, Trump said he might “at some point. But right now, I think the situation is so good.”

Later, he posted on Truth Social that he was preparing an economic crackdown meant to devastate Iran and any of its allies. “ANY country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences,” he wrote.

“This will be an ECONOMIC D-DAY,” he wrote, later adding: “IRAN WILL NEVER HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON.”

Denying Iran a nuclear weapon has been the only consistent message throughout the war. It’s what Iran hawks want the public to hear. But one House Republican who supports the war said that while it’s the right message, it can be difficult for the public to grasp the nuances of the dangers of nuclear enrichment.

Over the past few weeks, Trump has told his advisers he’s willing to wait to see how a strategy to further isolate Iran’s economy takes hold, according to a senior administration official. They said the president’s hope is to outlast the will of the Iranians, whom Trump has called “crazy motherfuckers” in private.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is expected to release a plan this week for economic penalties, which officials have called the most severe sanctions yet on actors who help fund Iran.

Mark Cancian, a defense expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, called the current phase a “battle of economic attrition.”

The U.S. could continue fighting Iran “for a considerable amount of time,” Cancian said. But the bigger problem is what each additional strike means for the U.S.'s overall capacity as a world power.

“Every missile that we use is one fewer that would be available for conflict in the Western Pacific,” he said.

Trump has also floated other options, including threatening to turn America's military power on Oman and to accelerate strikes on Iran, despite outside experts’ warnings to preserve more of the remaining stockpiles. The president has been briefed repeatedly on the stockpile of munitions, according to two sources familiar with the conversations, one of whom said the current arsenal is sufficient to carry out the plans Trump has been presented should he choose to escalate the war again.

The uncertainty has left some in the region with a grim conclusion: “They have no clear plan, unfortunately,” a Middle Eastern diplomat told NOTUS.

The mixed messages on what’s next are grating for some Americans, Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-North Dakota), a Trump ally, told NOTUS.

“One of the challenges is that people on either end of the spectrum — whether you’re a hardcore Iran hawk versus a geopolitical dove — you might get frustrated by the on-again, off-again use of lethality, followed by short stints of negotiation,” Cramer said. “But that’s not surprising to me with Donald Trump because, at the end of the day, he sees things through the lens of a negotiator and a transactional political figure.”

Sources close to Trump say the domestic pressures from the war are not a part of his calculus, but aides do consider them.

Surveys and polls show a slightly lower approval for Trump’s handling of the war than his overall approval rating, which hovers between 27% and 35%. A July 30 AP/NORC Center poll found that 64% of American adults believe the war hasn’t been worthwhile, and 72% want the U.S. to prioritize lowering gas prices. And many said they don’t even know what America is fighting for.

Even lawmakers who have received private briefings from the administration are unclear.

“What’s the endgame?” Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-Louisiana) said.

entries.title: Carter Barron’s Return
entries.content:
Good morning. This is the NOTUS Metro newsletter for Aug. 20, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

A famous federally owned performing arts center in D.C. is welcoming the public back.

No, we’re not talking about the Kennedy Center, but rather the Carter Barron Amphitheater in Rock Creek Park. Tonight kicks off a three-night concert series at the famed 76-year-old venue, which has been shuttered for almost a decade. (The Saturday show is sold out, but $15 tickets are available for tonight and Friday.)

The historic site — it was one of the country’s first integrated outdoor music venues, opened to celebrate the 150th anniversary of D.C. becoming the nation’s capital — is owned and operated by the National Park Service, but long suffered from deferred maintenance.

Dan Puskar is the executive director of the Rock Creek Conservancy, which is helping put on the concert series. He warns that the amphitheater remains “rough around the edges,” but thinks the concerts can serve to reintroduce residents to what was once a beloved institution.

“I hope we’ll see by the end of this weekend there is a model here, so that maybe we can begin doing more of these limited engagements,” he told NOTUS. “Washingtonians deserve to get into Carter Barron. If we can help make that happen, it would be a wonderful thing.”

Still, Carter Barron isn’t fully ready for prime time. Puskar estimates that just fixing its iconic stage could cost $10 million, while a full rehab of the venue could run more than $40 million. But he says making the investment could fit into President Donald Trump’s broader interest in renovating federal sites in D.C.

“It has been amazing to see the administration focus on D.C. in many different ways,” he said. “Could this be a part of it? Of course it could.”

And hey, the venue’s name already incorporates at least one Trump — Barron, that is.





DEEP DIVE

D.C. offers high school students more college tuition assistance than ever. Earlier this year, the city announced it’d increase an annual, congressionally funded grant program known as DCTAG that’s meant to cover the difference between in- and out-of-state tuition costs at public universities to a maximum of $15,000 — a $5,000 increase from a rate set in 1999.

But college costs have exploded in the past 27 years. Educators tell NOTUS’ Zara Norman that D.C.’s $5,000 increase is meaningful, and should allow many students to attend college without taking out loans — but it may not be enough.

“There should be something so [it’s not] every 25 years that we get an increase,” the CEO of another local scholarship program told NOTUS.

DC tuition assistance chart (1240x1150, AR: 1.08)




FROM THE DISTRICT

An update ahead of Trayon White’s September bribery trial: NOTUS’ Jenny Gathright reports that prosecutors asked the court on Wednesday to admonish the Ward 8 council member over a text they said his chief of staff sent to a government witness last week. The message, sent to Office of Neighborhood Safety and Engagement Director Kwelli Sneed, included a link to a news story listing the trial’s witnesses and said “Keeping you prayed up,” according to prosecutors.

The government’s lawyers called the message “a clear attempt to rattle or harass witnesses.” White’s attorney said it was the first he had heard of this message, and that he would speak to his client.

When reached for comment, chief of staff Sheila Bunn said she has a longstanding personal relationship with Sneed.

“I reached out to her purely in my personal capacity, as a friend and as a Christian woman, to check on someone I care about,” Bunn said. “My message was not intended to influence, intimidate, rattle, or sway her in any way, nor was it sent on behalf of council member White or his office.”

After a lengthy and at times contentious legal process, D.C.'s Office of the Attorney General has reached a settlement agreement with the mother of Deon Kay. Kay was fatally shot by D.C. police officer Alexander Alvarez in 2020, weeks after his 18th birthday. The settlement amount is $605,000, a spokesperson for the attorney general's office tells NOTUS, and the agreement awaits approval by a judge.

The tarp covering the Kennedy Center facade should remain as part of ongoing construction activities following the removal of Trump’s name from the building, Justice Department attorneys argued in a Tuesday court filing, NOTUS’ Jackie Llanos reports.

D.C.’s School Without Walls placed fifth in a new U.S. News and World Reportranking of the nation’s best high schools, jumping from 69th place last year,WTOP reports.




FROM VIRGINIA

Trump’s proposed renovation of Dulles International Airport got a big boost Wednesday, as the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority approved a $15.5 billion budget for the project, The Washington Post reports. Not included in those plans: a record-breaking parking garage.

Democratic Reps. Suhas Subramanyam and Don Beyer announced Wednesday there will be a joint investigation between the House Judiciary, Homeland Security and Oversight committees into the case of a Virginia woman confronted by an armed ICE agent last week.

In the minority, the Democrats do not have subpoena power and cannot force the Department of Homeland Security to comply with their investigation. Beyer told reporters Wednesday that he has not yet gotten any sign that DHS will cooperate.





TALK TO TOM

Each Peach - Chevre cheese (3000x2000, AR: 1.50)
Tom Sietsema is back answering your questions about the D.C. dining scene. Submit your questions here.

We love cheese and are so sad that there are few, if any, cheese shops in the D.C. area. Any thoughts? 

Your question sent me into the field — well, into some popular shops in the DMV — where I found extra options for you. Just this week, I admired how the owner of the neighborly Each Peach Market in Mount Pleasant sang the praises of the fluffy, subtly tangy, fresh chevre from Pipe Dreams I selected, then lamented that its longtime maker in Greencastle, Pennsylvania, was considering retirement. In Arlington, at the more expansive Arrowine & Cheese, the aroma at the door alone (pleasantly pungent) confirms you’re in the right place for fromage. A counter in the rear displays more than 130 selections.

Area cheese fanciers of my acquaintance also recommend the family-run Bowers Fancy Dairy Products stand at Eastern Market, a mainstay since 1964; La Jambe in Union Market; Calvert Woodley Fine Wines & Spirits, another of my go-to spots, usually before I’m having friends for happy hour; Gemelli’s Italian Market in Gaithersburg; Stonyman Gourmet Farmer in Kensington; and Piazza Italian Market in Easton, where a well-traveled food friend says she’s found some international cheeses that “I have never seen in this country.”

In the full Q&A: New spots for private dining, the reasons behind a rash of restaurant closures and recommendations from Down Under. 





SPORTS

Many baseball fans know Tommy John as the namesake of MLB’s most ubiquitous surgery. But John, who died last week at 83, was much more than that, NOTUS’ Thomas Boswell writes. He was a great pitcher, a good man and an honest quote. Once, late in John’s career, Boswell asked him if he felt a strong desire to chase 300 career wins. “The only thing that burns inside me,” the pitcher responded, “is Szechuan food.”

Training camp update: NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson reports that it seems increasingly unlikely Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels will see the field this preseason. Daniels was held out last week versus Miami and probably won't play next week against Baltimore because the teams have a joint practice two days prior. That leaves Saturday's game against Detroit. But if starting center Nick Allegretti (calf) isn't ready to play, there's little reason for Daniels to suit up.

"No decision yet," coach Dan Quinn said Wednesday. "We'll [decide] after we see the health of everybody."

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals at Rangers, 8:05 p.m. (MLB.TV)

entries.title: What Trump Wants
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Iran plans remain elusive. The latest White House press secretary goss. House campaign updates from Michigan and Pennsylvania. And: Darline Graham’s campaign cash haul. 





THE LATEST

If there’s an Iran plan, it’s a secret. Two House Republicans told NOTUS that they weren’t given talking points on the current status of the war by the White House before they left Washington for their August recess. A MAGA influencer who had been invited to private briefings with Vice President JD Vance and other top officials said the outreach has ceased and information is scarce. And it’s been more than 100 days since the Department of Defense held a press briefing.

Left in the dark are Donald Trump’s political allies, who not only want to help the president sell the Iran war but desperately need something substantive to say ahead of the fast-approaching midterms. NOTUS’ Jasmine Wright and colleagues tell the story of how the White House’s messaging — or lack thereof — on the war is affecting Trump’s most high-profile foreign policy move.

“How do we finish the job? It has not been answered yet,” Sen. Mike Rounds (R-South Dakota) told us.

Over the past few weeks, Trump has told his advisers he’s willing to wait to see how a strategy to further isolate Iran’s economy takes hold, according to a senior administration official. They said the president’s hope is to outlast the will of the Iranians, whom Trump has called “crazy motherfuckers” in private. “This will be Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale,” Trump posted last night.

The problem for the White House is that no one else seems to think this counts as a strategy. Maybe because no one has been told how it would work. “They have no clear plan, unfortunately,” a diplomat from a Middle Eastern country told NOTUS.

Open tabs: U.S. Debt Hits $40 Trillion as America’s Borrowing Binge Continues (NYT); Trump to be interviewed by Michael Cohen (MS NOW); Michigan Jewish Dems circulate letter endorsing Mike Rogers for Senate (Jewish Insider); Board overseeing Dulles Airport approves $15.5 billion to fund Trump renovation (WaPo)





From the White House


Scoop: Male spokesperson sought. Apply within. Trump has told close advisers he would prefer a man to fill Karoline Leavitt’s soon-to-be-vacant lectern, Jasmine and NOTUS’ Kadia Goba report. Among the men under consideration: CNN contributor Scott Jennings (Trump is not quite sold on the idea, a source familiar said) and Ari Fleischer, who served as press secretary to George W. Bush.

Or, perhaps, Trump could go a different way entirely. One source close to the White House predicted that all of the attention on the presidential aide Natalie Harp could catapult her into the position.

Trump word cloud: We’ve got charts! Violet Jira reports that Trump has said the word “Biden” more than he has any affordability-related word at 311 transcribed public appearances where at least one of the words was used. “Iran” is the most common word the president has uttered. Behind the numbers: Despite overwhelming evidence that affordability is defining the current political moment, the president is often reflexively dismissive of the issue when he does talk about it, Violet writes.

“President Trump can walk and chew gum at the same time,” a White House spokesperson told NOTUS. “As a result, the Trump Administration continues to deliver on the President’s affordability agenda by lowering drug prices, reshoring American jobs, and cutting taxes while simultaneously touting a historic drop in violent crime nationwide and the most secure border in history.”

From the campaign trail


First on NOTUS: Democratic poll shows a real race in Michigan’s 7th. Fresh numbers from House Majority PAC find Democratic nominee William Lawrence at 49% and Republican Rep. Tom Barrett at 47%. The poll had Barrett’s favorability rating in the district underwater, 35-47, and Trump’s at 43-53.

After the Democratic establishment wing could not pick between two candidates in the primary, progressive challenger Lawrence won the Democratic nomination to take on Barrett, who was elected to his seat by a 4-point margin in 2024. (Trump won the district by around 1 point.) The district is widely rated as a toss-up, and a prime Democratic pickup opportunity, but many see Lawrence’s win as giving Barrett some breathing room. Lawrence said after the primary that he let his DSA membership lapse to focus on uniting Democrats around his candidacy. As has been the case in many races this cycle, data centers have emerged as a central campaign focus.

Speaking of data centers, NOTUS’ Reese Gorman asked Speaker Mike Johnson about them yesterday while he campaigned in Pennsylvania with Rep. Rob Bresnahan. In recent weeks, Johnson has been a data center cheerleader, speaking out against any federal action preventing them from being built. But on the trail, he told Reese the federal government should “yield to local and state officials” when it comes to data center policy.

Bresnahan echoed a growing bipartisan distaste for the projects. “There are some communities across the country that have embraced AI data centers, and there are some, just like here in northeastern Pennsylvania, that are vehemently against it for rightful reasons,” he said.







NOTUS PERSPECTIVES

Last Saturday, in response to a public invitation, about 1,000 people showed up in Meridian Hill Park to eat apples. Anusha Mathur of NOTUS Perspectives went to witness the scene — and concluded that it said something surprising about Washington in 2026. Plus: Matt K. Lewis argues that Reagan worship is obsolete, and it’s time for Republicans toanoint a new historical hero: Teddy Roosevelt.

NEW ON NOTUS

Sen. Darline Graham made a hefty campaign cash haul just days after being sworn into her late brother’s Senate seat, from chief executives, lobbyists and other prominent Republican donors. Some of them opened their wallets a little too wide, NOTUS’ Mark Alfred reports. Graham took in more than $24,000 worth of contributions over the max limit, according to an FEC letter to her campaign.

Graham’s campaign now has to return or redistribute the money, which accounts for 10% of her cash on hand.

entries.content:
Welcome to Talk to Tom, the dining advice column that aims to point you toward good meals, steer you from the dross and solve your pressing restaurant queries.

Look for a fresh Q&A every Thursday in this space. Questions and comments can be submitted to TalkToTom@notus.com. Submissions may be edited for length and clarity.

I’m an event scheduler, looking for some new ideas for smallish private dining in D.C. I’m interested in somewhere other than the usual steak houses and hotel venues. 

Let me direct you to the hot-hot Uchi, the dashing Japanese import from Austin, which offers two separate spaces, one with room for 14, the other with seats for eight — both of which can be accessed via a private entrance for those who want to play like VIPs; the Italian newcomer Rosselli, whose 10-seat La Vigna off the main dining room is fronted with mesh metal curtains and decorated with a mural of a vineyard; and Barbouzard, the sweeping Mediterranean retreat from top chef Cedric Maupillier. The last has several options, the most intimate of which is the window-wrapped Royale Champagne Parlor with plush seats for 16 guests and a view into the kitchen.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Each Peach - Chevre cheese (3000x2000, AR: 1.50)
We love cheese and are so sad that there are few, if any, cheese shops in the D.C. area. There’s Cheesetique in Alexandria and a few vendors at the farmers market, so we end up ordering from Goldbelly, the online national food source. Any thoughts? 

Your question sent me into the field — well, into some popular shops in the DMV — where I found extra options for you. Just this week, I admired how the owner of the neighborly Each Peach Market in Mount Pleasant sang the praises of the fluffy, subtly tangy, fresh chevre from Pipe Dreams I selected, then lamented that its longtime maker in Greencastle, Pennsylvania, was considering retirement. In Arlington, at the more expansive Arrowine & Cheese, the aroma at the door alone (pleasantly pungent) confirms you’re in the right place for fromage. A counter in the rear displays more than 130 selections. “I counted them once,” says the staff member who assisted me with my requests for a cheese that would be appropriate for a sandwich in someone’s office and something richer and runnier for home consumption. Just as a sommelier might pour a taste for a diner considering a bottle of wine, the attendant offered previews of the Alpine Knock Out (love the hint of mushrooms and white pepper in the finish) and buttery, salty Époisses coupe. Its surface looks like a brain; the texture is so runny, it practically melts at room temperature.

Area cheese fanciers of my acquaintance also recommend the family-run Bowers Fancy Dairy Products stand at Eastern Market, a mainstay since 1964; La Jambe in Union Market; Calvert Woodley Fine Wines & Spirits, another of my go-to spots, usually before I’m having friends for happy hour; Gemelli’s Italian Market in Gaithersburg; Stonyman Gourmet Farmer in Kensington; and Piazza Italian Market in Easton, where a well-traveled food friend says she’s found some international cheeses that “I have never seen in this country.”

By the way, a good cheesemonger is likely to ask what you plan to do with the cheese; offer tastes of a product before you buy it; cut cheese to order rather than as a wrapped product; and use cheese paper instead of plastic film, which suffocates the cheese. Try the sniff test in the shop, too. Earthy and even barnyard-y aromas are appropriate. Ammonia or sour smells raise a reg flag.

Each Peach Owner (3504x2336, AR: 1.50)
I’ve noticed more restaurants closing recently, especially those that have been around awhile. What’s the driver behind this? 

There are many factors at play, restaurateurs tell me. Downtown, Chinatown and Penn Quarter have been hit especially hard by the failure of workers not returning to their offices, for instance. Federal job cuts and agency downsizing have also contributed to the closures. Rising costs across the board — food, insurance, labor — mean ever-smaller margins for operators. (In a competitive market, some dishwashers make north of $20.) Layer on staffing issues, chefs and landlords who can’t agree to terms, and fewer international visitors to the city, and it’s a wonder more businesses don’t shutter.

Finally, when the cost of living goes up, guess what people cut from their budget first? Eating out.

It’s great to see your writing and recommendations again! My wife and I will be in Sydney for our honeymoon in December and January. We’re big foodies, but we prefer food quality and restaurant vibes to fine dining per se. 

I’ve never been Down Under, but I know someone who lives there and covers the food scene in Sydney: Jenifer Jagielski, the byline behind “Eat Street” in the Sunday Telegraph and other publications. (You can find her at sydneyeatstreet on Instagram.) In general, “Sydney is renowned for its seafood, particularly the Sydney rock oysters,” Jagielski says. The city also has a large Asian population, “so you’ll find lots of ‘[culturally]-inspired’ cuisines,” she adds.

Her short list includes:

Tam Jiak, in the redeveloped Sydney Fish Market, for Malaysian cooking built around a surf-and-turf concept. Every dish has a land and sea element. (The roast duck, for instance, is black from a brush with squid ink.)

Spice Temple, for modern Chinese with Sichuan, Yunnan and Hunan accents, in a scene-y dining room.

Aalia, near the famous Opera House, which showcases Middle Eastern small plates.

Nomad, another casual, ingredient-focused Middle Eastern and Mediterranean dining room with the bonus of a good wine list.

Bennelong, set in one of the “sails” of the Opera House and spanning three levels. Look for contemporary Australian fare, a raw bar and multiple ways to eat, including from a pre-theater list.

Mr. Wong, a lively, two-level Cantonese restaurant where dim sum and barbecued duck are among the signatures.

La Favola in nearby Newtown, whose chef grew up outside Naples and where the small menu is a handful of pastas and toppings made from scratch daily.

Jagielski didn’t just provide food tips. “Dress codes aren’t really a thing here,” she wrote me. Also, “contrary to what people have heard about not tipping in Australia, alas, the U.S.’s influence has begun to normalize tipping in restaurants.” Fifteen to 20% is “appreciated” now, she says.

entries.title: D.C. Gives High Schoolers More College Tuition Assistance Than Ever. Is It Enough?
entries.summary: To bridge the gap between in- and out-of-state costs, the grant now provides up to $15,000 a year.
entries.content:
Clarence Cross was in high school when D.C. launched its tuition assistance grant program in 1999. By the time the program’s dollar value increased one cent, he was an educator himself.

The program, D.C. Tuition Assistance Grant (DCTAG), gives thousands of the District’s high school students money to help pay for out-of-state tuition at public universities, since D.C. has only one — the University of the District of Columbia, ranked 145th among northern region universities by U.S. News and World Report.

“It really just provides a lot of access for our students, especially first-generation, low-income students,” Cross, an associate director at Friendship Public Charter School in Northwest D.C., told NOTUS.

When the congressionally funded program was introduced, its annual award, capped at $10,000, largely covered the gap between in- and out-of-state tuition rates at regional public colleges. At the time, tuition at the University of Maryland’s flagship campus cost $6,888 more for out-of-state students, and George Mason University cost $8,760 more.

But costs have exploded since then, and D.C. has the highest average student loan debt in the country at $54,561, according to 2026 data from the Education Data Initiative. Today, Maryland’s out-of-state tuition costs $31,252 more per year than in-state. At George Mason, the difference is $24,996. That’s before additional costs like housing and food.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

To catch up, this February DCTAG saw its first-ever increase, from a maximum of $10,000 to $15,000 a year, with its lifetime cap raised to $75,000 instead of $50,000.

“The latest projections show that the average award amount will increase from approximately $7,700 a year to $12,500 a year,” a spokesperson for D.C.’s Office of the State Superintendent of Education, which administers DCTAG, told NOTUS in a statement.

Educators say it’s a meaningful increase.

“For some of our kids, [it] was really exactly what they needed to make sure that they could go to college with no significant bill or tuition or having to take out loans. For [others], it has closed the gap pretty significantly,” Mashea Ashton, the founder and CEO of local charter school Digital Pioneers Academy, told NOTUS.

But even at $15,000 a year, the program doesn’t close that gap entirely.

DC tuition assistance chart (1240x1150, AR: 1.08)
Those rates are eye-popping, but the sticker price can often be reduced for low- and middle-income students, said Preston Magouirk, a senior executive at local scholarship program DC CAP. The nonprofit gives selected D.C. high schoolers thousands of dollars annually to attend college, with a dedicated program for students in Wards 7 and 8.

“There are some people that can pay those high premiums, but for the vast majority of students, that's not what's asked,” Magouirk told NOTUS.

For those middle- and low-income students, DCTAG is one tile in a mosaic of aid they rely on for assistance, one that can include Pell Grants, additional scholarships like those offered by DC CAP or a school’s own financial aid packages, Magouirk said. Or, they take out loans.

“If their families are in a position to be able to take out loans, then their families do, and it is definitely a huge financial burden for both the family and the kid,” Ashton said. “[Some] decide to just go to work, or stay local and go to the University of the District of Columbia with the goal that after a year, they'll be able to either save more money or get more scholarships so that they can transfer to their dream college or university.”

It would take federal action to expand the program further, the superintendent office spokesperson told NOTUS. That’s what happened this past year.

Ashton suggested increasing tuition assistance not just for D.C. students who want to attend public universities, but also for those who want to attend private, higher-cost, historically Black colleges and universities. And Eric Waldo, the CEO of the DC CAP scholarship program, proposed tying DCTAG increases to the cost of inflation.

“There should be something so [it’s not] every 25 years that we get an increase,” Waldo told NOTUS. “We could get our arms around this problem. Last year, 4,100 students graduated from D.C. schools. That's a small group. Only about 840 or so are economically disadvantaged who are going to college. We should be able to serve all of them.”

entries.title: ‘Affordability’ Is This Year’s Buzzword. Just Not When Trump’s Talking.
entries.summary: As Americans struggle to afford the basics, the president keeps touting the hot economy and the need for a White House ballroom.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump spoke to a crowd of families in late July at a high school in Marietta, Georgia.

He talked about Venezuelan oil and the war in Iran. He ticked off investment commitments. And he touted provisions in the Republican tax bill — or tried to.

“This past filing season, 130,000 tipped workers right here in Georgia saved an average of more than $7,000 on their taxes. And that’s because of no tax on tips. You know, we’re building a tremendous military facility at the White House,” Trump said. “And they’ve been working hard, a lot of overtime.”

The speech in a state that will be pivotal in November was one of a handful Trump has delivered this year, part of what White House chief of staff Susie Wiles said in January would be weekly trips across the country to talk to voters ahead of the midterms.

Last month, the Pew Research Center asked voters what they most wanted to hear about from candidates. The answer was overwhelmingly cost of living, wages and affordability. More than half of voters think the economy is getting worse, according to a July Quinnipiac University poll. And 58% of those polled disapproved of Trump’s handling of the economy.

A March report found that nearly half of families do not make enough to cover the basic cost of living in their communities. Only 13% of Americans aged 18-29 believe the country is headed in the right direction, according to Harvard’s youth poll that was conducted last November.

But despite overwhelming evidence that affordability is defining the current political moment, the president is often reflexively dismissive of the issue.

“‘What are you going to do about the prices?’” Trump recounted in Georgia of a question he says he’s often asked. “They used a word — first time I heard it — it was a word made up by the Democrats: affordability. They said affordability.”

This is overwhelmingly the context in which Trump mentions affordability, a NOTUS review of Trump’s speaking events this year using Roll Call’s Factbase found. Republicans across the board say that Trump is instrumental to any win in November. But he rarely acknowledges the issue that will decide the election.

https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/seRx9/full.pngTrump’s mentions of key economic terms are rarely in the context of affordability. When the president uses the word “prices,” it is often to say that his administration inherited high prices and has worked to lower them.

“You know, and they have this term. So here I am, I’m one day in office and the fake news goes, ‘affordability, affordability.’ I said, ‘What’s that all about?’ ‘Prices are too high,’ I said, ‘I’m here for less than 24 hours,’” Trump told a crowd in Milford, Michigan, in July. “But we’ve brought down prices. Last week, it was announced that inflation has gone down faster than at any time in the last six years.”

A superlative almost always precedes Trump’s mentions of the economy — Trump frequently refers to the economy of his first term as “the greatest economy ever” and similarly praises his second-term economy.

“I proudly signed the largest tax cuts in American history for the second time, because in my first term, we had the greatest economy in the history of our country,” Trump said in Michigan. “Didn’t get credit, but that’s OK. But we had the greatest economy in the history of the country. And we’re blowing it away this time.”

While the economy may look broadly good on paper — the stock market is performing well and unemployment is low — Americans across the country are struggling with high housing costs, soaring grocery prices and wages that aren’t keeping up with inflation. For many households, the disconnect between economic indicators and their personal finances has continued to worsen.

Anne Hamming, the communications manager at Feeding America West Michigan, told NOTUS that her local branch of the hunger relief organization is seeing a higher rate of childhood food insecurity, which she said indicates that higher costs are squeezing families.

In lower-wage households, Hamming said, small increases in grocery costs or a trip to the gas station “make an impact.”

“They add up,” she said. “We hear all over the place that people are just really struggling.”

Bureau of Labor Statistics data released Wednesday paints this same picture in numbers: An increase in prices wiped out wage gains. Inflation and high energy prices, a result of the war in Iran, have added to the squeeze and worsened the cost-of-living problems plaguing many Americans.

In a statement to NOTUS, White House spokesperson Olivia Wales did not acknowledge NOTUS’ questions about the frequency of cost-of-living issues in the president’s statements.

“President Trump can walk and chew gum at the same time,” she said. “As a result, the Trump Administration continues to deliver on the President’s affordability agenda by lowering drug prices, reshoring American jobs, and cutting taxes while simultaneously touting a historic drop in violent crime nationwide and the most secure border in history.”

https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/Jyj7s/full.pngThe White House signaled an intention to focus on affordability and the midterms late last year.

“The president is very keyed into what’s going on, and he recognizes, like anybody, that it takes time to do an economic turnaround, but all the fundamentals are there, and I think you’ll see him be very, very focused on prices and cost of living,” former White House deputy chief of staff James Blair told Politico last November.

But for much of this year, other issues have captured a larger share of the president’s remarks — most notably the war in Iran and related foreign policy issues. The war is unpopular: A Politico poll conducted by Public First found that support for the war is slipping even among Trump’s most ardent supporters.

“With the economy, the biggest issue is two things. Number one, the discipline and consistency in talking about the wins that you’re having in the economy. The administration lacks a certain discipline that you get from mainstream administrations,” Cory Ruth, a Republican strategist, and industry consultancy company CEO in Georgia, told NOTUS. “The second thing is, there are people in his administration that are highly politicized, and the media is never going to take them at face value. And then there are people in the administration who the media does respect and does listen to. They’re less politicized, and he doesn’t do a good job of putting those people up front.”

The White House has undertaken efforts aimed at answering the affordability question. For example, it rolled out TrumpRx, a prescription drug website designed to offer deals on medication. But NOTUS found that Trump has only mentioned TrumpRx at eight speaking events since the platform launched in February.

While Congressional Republicans refer to last year’s tax bill as the “Working Families Tax Cuts Act,” Trump continues to call it the “Big, Beautiful Bill.” While he talks about its provisions like no tax on tips, which Republicans acknowledge are more popular than the legislation as a whole, he mentioned them in less than 20% of all transcribed speaking events this year.

“He ended taxes on overtime. If you are a sort of blue-collar worker or a working-class person, and you … are allowed to get overtime, that’s gone. And so there are things that he’s doing,” Ruth said, adding that the drumbeat of that messaging “is just not consistent enough.”

Before departing on a trip to China in May, Trump was asked whether he was taking into account Americans’ financial situations as he tried to negotiate an end to the Iran war.

“I don’t think about Americans’ financial situation, I don’t think about anybody,” Trump said. “I think about one thing. We can not let Iran have a nuclear weapon. That’s all. That’s the only thing that matters.”

Republicans previously told NOTUS that they were frustrated with that response, and with the way that he talks about the economy broadly. Democrats, on the other hand, said they have every intention of capitalizing on Trump’s perceived lack of concern.

“Americans’ financial situation is dire, and Republicans don’t think about anyone other than Donald Trump,” Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer said the next day.

Note: Sampled words may represent a combination of multiple terms. For example, “affordability” includes instances where the president said “afford,” “affordable,” and affordability. Others are as follows: costs (cost/costs/cost of living), wages (wage/wages/paycheck/pocket), economy (economy/economic), price (price/prices), and families (Family/families). 

Some statements were omitted based on context. For example, Trump saying on Feb. 20 that some Supreme Court justices were an “embarrassment to their families” was not included in the count for the term families, as families in that context is not related to affordability.

entries.title: The Mystics Value Georgia Amoore’s Intangibles. They’d Also Gladly Take More Points.
entries.summary: There’s little doubt Washington is at its best when the rookie point guard is at hers.
entries.content:
At the end of an unremarkable Washington Mystics shootaround, on the first of six game days in a span of a week and a half, near the end of the fourth month of a grueling, five-month season, Georgia Amoore took it upon herself to break the morning monotony. Upon nailing her heave in the team’s daily half-court shooting contest, the Mystics’ rookie point guard ripped off her practice jersey, waved it over her head and sprinted away in her sports bra, Brandi Chastain-style, leaving her teammates doubled over in laughter.

It was classic Amoore: boundless energy, pure fun, unadulterated spirit. Pro basketball is hard, as the 25-year-old Australia native would be the first to tell you. But that doesn’t mean it has to be joyless.

In the midst of a special season for the Mystics, as the youngest team in the WNBA closes in on a playoff berth, Amoore’s struggles on the court have stood out like 6-foot-7 center Lauren Betts in a room full of second-graders.

With that in mind, of all the developments for the Mystics in Wednesday night’s 93-82 home win over the injury-depleted Toronto Tempo, the biggest was arguably Amoore’s productive night: nine points on 3-of-6 shooting, plus three assists. It may not look like much, but those nine points tripled her production over the previous five games, in which her point totals, respectively, were zero, zero, zero, three and zero.

“Yes, we need her to make threes. We need her to guard her matchup. We need her to find [open] people,” Mystics coach Sydney Johnson said of Amoore. “Those are all the stats and performance part. And that’s critical, because it’s the pros. But what she gives to us, whether that [performance] is on or off, is connectivity. And that’s why she’s such a key player for us. She’s a key part of what we’ve got going this year. We wouldn’t be here without her.”

Since falling to .500 in mid-July, the Mystics have now won nine of their past 11 games, the only blemishes a pair of road losses at defending champion Las Vegas. And with Saturday’s win against Los Angeles, the Mystics have the distinction of beating every team in the league at least once.

Georgia Amoore AP - 26180416398171 (3900x2610, AR: 1.49)
With just nine regular-season games remaining (seven of them against teams from the bottom half of the standings), the Mystics, among the most pleasant surprises of this WNBA season, control their own playoff destiny. In seventh place at 21-14, and six games clear of ninth-place Portland, they are closer (two games) to a berth in the top four, which would guarantee home-court advantage in the best-of-three first round, than they are to falling clear out of the playoff picture.

Plenty of observers expected the Mystics to deal for a veteran point guard at the trade deadline earlier this month, given the lack of production from Amoore and backup Alicia Florez. But rather than give up a piece of its future for a boost to its present, the franchise stayed true to its mission of building a consistent contender through drafting and player development — even if it meant the Mystics might be a piece or two shy of true title contention in 2026.

Their only move was a low-risk waiver claim on 32-year-old wing Betnijah Laney-Hamilton, late of the New York Liberty, who automatically became the oldest player on the Mystics’ roster by a whopping eight years — as well as the only player on the team with a WNBA championship ring, earned with New York in 2024. (She also juiced the roster’s average age to the point where they are no longer the second-youngest team in WNBA history, but merely the 10th-youngest.)

While the Mystics’ failure to import a new point guard could have been interpreted as a vote of confidence in Amoore, it was shortly after the trade deadline that her performance bottomed out, as she went a combined 1-for-17 from the floor during the stretch of five games in which she scored a total of just three points. In the last of those five games, at home against Los Angeles on Saturday, she played a season-low 11 minutes and was again on the bench in the latter moments of the game.

But the Mystics have been unyielding in backing Amoore publicly, taking pains to point out all the things she does that don’t show up on the stats sheet — shouting it louder the more she struggled on the court. This week, Johnson singled her out when asked to name his most underrated player.

“She is really key in terms of executing what we want to do offensively and defensively,” Johnson said Wednesday. “And yeah, her playing time is going to fluctuate, because there are other players out there helping us as well. [But] her ability to keep us connected and keep us true to the scouting report, essentially operating as a coach on the floor, has been off the charts. Off the charts.”

There’s little doubt the Mystics are at their best when Amoore is at hers. It’s no coincidence some of her best performances have come in some of the Mystics’ most impressive wins: 10 points and eight assists in a road win against New York in June, eight and seven in another road win at Minnesota two days later; nine and eight in a win at Golden State in July; 12 and five in a home win against Dallas two weeks ago.

But in recent weeks, as Amoore’s slump deepened, the Mystics have frequently kept her on the bench in crunch time, with Sonia Citron, a wing by trade, shifting into the point guard role — despite her own reservations over it. It happened again Wednesday night, with Amoore and Florez both on the bench and Citron shifting to point guard whenever the Tempo made a run that threatened the Mystics’ lead.


“We’re tremendously different” when Amoore is on her game, Citron said. “She has such a big impact, and it goes way beyond whether she’s making shots or not, or the number of points she has. She’s a great leader. She’s a great captain. She gets us into our offense. … For me, I just feel a lot more at peace and calm when she’s on the floor, knowing she’s going to get our team in shape and get us where we need to go.”


Georgia Amoore AP - 26129014215337 (5561x3812, AR: 1.46)
Amoore, Citron said, “sees things other people don't see, whether that’s calling for something — telling the post, ‘Go screen down for Sonia’ — that’s not really a play. That’s just something she sees. And that’s something I don't do. When I run the offense, I call a play, and that’s what it is. Whereas she reads the game — a point guard mentality.”

Amoore, a first-round draft pick (sixth overall) out of Kentucky in 2025, tore her ACL three practices into her Mystics career and missed the entire season, meaning she is technically still a WNBA rookie. Now 15 months out from surgery, she acknowledges she is still building back strength and resilience in the joint.

“My knee, it’s stable. But I'm going through the ups and downs of building that tolerance back up again, trusting it again,” she said. “Obviously there’ve been some bumps and bruises along the way. It’s not a perfect process.”

In the meantime, she said, she makes an effort to pay attention to the things that don’t require perfect physical condition: body language, energy level, communication.

“That's a super undervalued part of the game,” Amoore said. “Sometimes it’s not real rewarding, but it’s needed. Obviously, I would love to have some [positive] stats to back that up. But … my body is getting used to the season again. If I was always super negative about how I'm feeling physically, which a lot of people fall into that trap, I wouldn't be much fun to be around. I’ve always been positive, always brought energy. And my performance is never going to affect that.”

There is no metric for measuring a player’s psychic contribution to a team’s mood, but if there were, Amoore’s value would be at an All-Star level. Whenever and wherever the Mystics are clowning around, which is basically always and anywhere, she is typically at the center of it, the full-sprinting, jersey-waving ringleader of this circus.

In the absence of compelling statistical evidence, that psychic value may not be enough to keep Amoore on the floor late in close games, and it may not be enough to keep the Mystics from prioritizing a point guard this offseason.

But it will keep Amoore around for a while. And when Amoore is around, running the offense, dishing out assists, turning random late-season shootarounds into slapstick comedy, the Mystics are a little bit better and a whole lot happier.

entries.title: Treasury Doubles Down on Its Plan to Stabilize Financial Markets
entries.summary: The bond markets rebounded to uncomfortable highs just a day after the Treasury Department announced a $4 billion buyback plan.
entries.content:
The Trump administration’s attempts to stabilize financial markets fizzled on Thursday, leading Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to suggest that a greater intervention may be on the way.

The Trump administration will announce plans in the coming days to potentially increase the $4 billion program to buy back government bonds from investors he first proposed yesterday, Bessent said Thursday.

The Trump administration’s initial plan to tamp down investor return rates didn’t work, with yields rebounding to uncomfortable highs on Thursday morning. The administration indicated it is planning to double down on the buyback program.

“We're going to increase the size of the buyback,” Bessent said on CNBC on Thursday morning. “We believe that the yields don't reflect the underlying fundamentals.”

Bessent added that the Trump administration will soon announce an “increased focus on fiscal consolidation,” a debt- and budget-slashing effort that will involve President Donald Trump and Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought.

Elon Musk’s DOGE commission, which led to sweeping federal workforce reductions and put billions of dollars in grants on hold, failed to hit its debt-reduction targets. Inflationary pressures driving bond market volatility appear unlikely to subside as Trump ratchets up pressure on Iran and threatens the adversary with “economic warfare.”

Bessent attempted to assuage concerns about inflation on Thursday, saying the U.S. “will get on the other side” of the war in Iran and calling government expenditures on factories, equipment and farms an “investment in the future,” rather than government spending. He expressed optimism that tariff refunds winding down and an increase in the tax base will help balance the government’s costs and revenue.

“Think of it as pulling back the slingshot here. We have a lot of potential energy that will turn into kinetic energy during this year,” Bessent said, adding that “there’s a very good chance” the U.S. has already seen the peak that the federal deficit will reach during this administration.

The Trump administration will hold a press conference Monday to discuss next steps on inflation, he said.

Yields had cratered on Wednesday following the Treasury’s announcement of an expanded buyback operation, which will take billions of dollars of government debt off the market and free up capital for investors anxious about the government’s ability to repay.

That progress came undone Thursday morning. Yields neared or exceeded the high bond rates that have plagued markets over the past several weeks and sparked fears of an approaching crisis. High yields mean higher borrowing costs for everyday Americans and businesses.

Economists expressed skepticism that the Treasury’s buyback tactic will solve the big-picture issues in the bond market, including inflationary pressures from Trump’s war in Iran and trade policy, as well as the rapid buildout of artificial intelligence.

“The market was perhaps reacting yesterday positively to signs that certain markets are going to have more liquidity, but today the markets have incorporated information and understand the long-term drivers of bond prices and yields have not changed,” said Judge Glock, the research director at the conservative Manhattan Institute.

“Absent some incredible change at the Federal Reserve or absent some incredible change in Congress that actually starts to reduce the federal deficit, those longer-term drivers likely will not change,” Glock added.

Economists who spoke with NOTUS on Thursday said an increased buyback program is not going to meet the bar for tempering the market’s volatility.

“If we're talking about kind of more permanently anchoring and lowering long-term bond yields, I think it's going to be quite ineffective,” said Alex Jacquez, a senior vice president at the left-leaning Groundwork Collaborative. “The market is incredibly right to be worried about what the president is going to do day-to-day.”

Jared Bernstein, a senior fellow at the left-leaning Center for American Progress who served as President Joe Biden’s chief economic adviser, said before Bessent’s Thursday remarks that an increased buyback “will do more harm than good, will smack of desperation, and will spook markets.”

However, the U.S.’s fiscal issues are deepening as the bond market grows increasingly unruly for the Trump administration. The national debt surpassed $40 trillion for the first time on Wednesday.

“There's nothing magic about the 40 trillion number, and we can grow our way out of that,” Bessent said.

The 30-year U.S. Treasury bonds dipped more than 10 basis points to as low as 5.183% in the hours after Bessent’s announcement Wednesday. It recovered 7 basis points at its highest point Thursday morning.

Yields over the past month have surpassed those during the 2007 financial crisis, leading Trump to blame high interest rates. The president has repeatedly called for the Fed to slash rates and pressured the previous Fed chair, Jerome Powell to get it done.

“We have interest rates that are artificially — they're actually artificially high,” Trump told reporters Wednesday. “They raise them for no reason, and you can't go out to the market when you have a Fed that's raising interest. You can't say, ‘I want to pay 3 points less than what the Fed says you're supposed to be paying.’”

entries.title: Lawmakers Sound the Alarm After Leadership Shake-up at Military Newspaper
entries.summary: A trio of Democratic senators said they were recently informed the Pentagon unilaterally changed a senior leadership position.
entries.content:
A trio of Democratic senators voiced concerns Thursday over the Pentagon’s controversial oversight of Stars and Stripes, a military newspaper partially funded by the federal government, after clashes over the publication’s editorial independence and its longtime publisher’s abrupt retirement announcement this week.

Max Lederer, who served as publisher for 19 years, announced his retirement Tuesday in a memo to the news organization’s staff, saying that his “understanding of the value and mission of Stars and Stripes” contrasted in “fundamental ways” from Pentagon leadership’s vision. He elaborated in an interview with Stars and Stripes on Wednesday that he particularly opposed the Pentagon’s plans to shift the outlet to a digital-only format.

Lederer’s announcement is the latest development in a string of turmoil that has engulfed the storied publication, which was originally created during the Civil War and revived during World War I.

Pentagon leadership under the Trump administration canceled the use of news wire services such as The Associated Press and Reuters. They also banned cartoons and other syndicated content. The publication’s ombudsman, Jacqueline Smith, was fired in April after calling the changes an infringement of Stars and Stripes’ editorial independence in an op-ed.

In a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Connecticut), Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts) and Jeanne Shaheen (D-New Hampshire) said they were recently informed that the Department of Defense had assigned an active-duty public affairs officer to serve as deputy for Lederer, reportedly without consultation.

The leadership change, they added, would further erode the publication’s credibility. They requested answers by Aug. 28 as to who appointed the public affairs officer to the position, what the officer’s duties would entail and what safeguards would be put in place to ensure there would be no interference by the Pentagon with the publication’s editorial decisions.

“For generations, American servicemembers, particularly those stationed overseas and in combat zones, have relied on Stars and Stripes for credible and independent news,” the letter read. “That trust depends on preserving a clear separation between independent journalism and the Department’s public affairs apparatus. At this critical moment of leadership transition, that independence must not be compromised.”

On Thursday, CBS News reported that the Pentagon was considering firing Lederer prior to his scheduled retirement.

The Defense Department did not immediately return a request for comment on the lawmakers’ letter, whether it was considering firing Lederer or on the decision-making behind his retirement.

Defense Department spokesperson Sean Parnell said in January that Stars and Stripes was returning to “its original mission.”

“We are bringing Stars & Stripes into the 21st century,” Parnell wrote. “We will modernize its operations, refocus its content away from woke distractions that syphon morale, and adapt it to serve a new generation of service members.”

entries.title: Judge Hands Republicans a Big Win in Missouri Redistricting Case
entries.summary: The state’s Republican Party is pushing for their redrawn maps to be used in this year’s midterm elections.
entries.content:
A Missouri judge handed Republicans a win in Missouri’s ongoing redistricting battle, as the state’s GOP pushes for their redrawn maps to be used in this year’s midterm elections.

In a ruling Wednesday, Cole County Judge Daniel Green upheld Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins’ decision earlier this month that blocked a referendum seeking to overturn the state’s new congressional maps. The lines had been redrawn to more heavily favor Republicans.

Missouri Republicans were one of the first delegations to take up President Donald Trump’s call last summer to redraw congressional maps in the hopes that Republicans could pad their numbers in this year’s midterm elections and hold control of the House of Representatives.

The party quickly pushed new Trump-backed maps through the state legislature, targeting long-serving Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver’s seat by splitting up parts of Kansas City.

Over 30,000 Missouri residents signed a petition seeking to force a statewide vote on the gerrymander, according to the organizing group, which handed in the signatures to Hoskins in December. In Missouri, a petition with enough signatures triggers a referendum on the law in question.

On Aug. 4, Hoskins, a Republican, rejected the petition that would have triggered a statewide vote on the new maps, calling the challenge itself unconstitutional.

In the decision issued Wednesday, Green said that because the Missouri Constitution doesn’t explicitly allow or instruct a referendum on redistricting, the referendum is not valid.

“Missouri has never — by constitutional provision, by statute, or by practice — subjected congressional redistricting to the referendum,” Green wrote. “At every turn where the question might have been addressed, Missouri’s framers and legislators either remained silent or affirmatively rejected referenda on redistricting.”

Green also wrote that he believed federal law would prohibit any changes to the maps so close to the general election, in part because the new maps were already used in the state’s primaries.

“An order changing the congressional map would thus create two classes of voters — those who had the opportunity to select their general election candidate and those who did not — in direct violation of the Equal Protection Clause,” Green wrote, stating that the court would not be making any changes to the new maps.

People Not Politicians, the group leading the lawsuit against the maps, vowed to fight the ruling in the state’s Supreme Court.

"The most important thing that happened today is that there was a ruling,” Richard von Glahn, the group’s executive director, said in a statement. “The State has tried to slow down the judicial process for months and now that we are out of Cole County, the real decision will be made. Our case now moves forward.”

Ballots for Missouri’s general election must be finalized by Sept. 8. Chief Justice Brent Powell ordered an expedited review of the case, with oral arguments set for Sept. 2.

entries.title: FBI Raids Eric Swalwell’s Home as Part of Sexual Assault Probe
entries.summary: Agents seized his electronic devices and raided his D.C. home over the weekend, according to reports.
entries.content:
FBI agents seized electronic devices from former California Rep. Eric Swalwell and raided his D.C. home last weekend in connection with an investigation into sexual assault allegations against him, according to multiple reports.

The execution of the search warrants at the San Francisco airport Saturday and his D.C. residence on Sunday were first reported by the Daily Mail Thursday and confirmed by other news outlets.

The Justice Department is investigating the allegations that led to Swalwell’s resignation from office and withdrawal from the California governor race in April, NOTUS previously reported. District attorneys in New York and Los Angeles also have ongoing probes.

A former staffer said he sexually assaulted her twice while she was intoxicated, and a former Capitol Hill intern told NOTUS that the former lawmaker had messaged her sexual advances on Snapchat.

At least five women have accused him of sexual assault and harassment. In the statement announcing his resignation, Swalwell vowed to fight the allegations, calling them false.

The FBI declined to comment, and his attorney did not respond to a request for comment.

This is a breaking story and will be updated.

entries.title: Top DHS Lawyer’s ‘Worst of the Worst’ Judges List Lands Him in Hot Water
entries.summary: More than 100 former judges say James Percival’s online behavior increases “the risk of violence” against them.
entries.content:
The top lawyer for the Department of Homeland Security is facing a bar complaint over an incendiary series of social media posts in which he listed and criticized federal judges who have ruled against the Trump administration.

In a complaint to the Florida Bar this week, lawyer groups and more than 100 former federal and state judges called for an investigation into DHS General Counsel James Percival, who started a “Worst of the Worst, District Judge Edition” series of posts on X in July. The language paralleled the administration’s public lists of undocumented immigrants who had committed or were accused of committing crimes.

Percival claimed that federal judges who ruled against the Trump administration were engaging in judicial sabotage and mutiny against the Supreme Court.

But the former judges argued he mischaracterized or falsely portrayed the cases.

“These statements, and similar statements Mr. Percival has made about other sitting judges, not only constitute serious professional misconduct, but they threaten the rule of law and increase the risk of violence against judges,” the complaint from the Democracy Defenders Fund, Lawyers Defending American Democracy and the former judges states.

Percival has dismissed concerns about the potential for inciting threats against judges, describing his posts as fact-based critiques. But in response to the bar complaint, Percival directed his focus on former Florida Supreme Court Chief Justice Peggy Quince. Her signature, as a board member of Lawyers Defending American Democracy, appears first on the complaint.

“In honor of former Florida Supreme Court Justice Peggy Quince, who just filed a bar complaint against me for calling out judicial activism, I will be creating a new award,” Percival posted on X Wednesday. “The award is called the Justice Peggy Quince Lifetime Achievement Award for Worst of the Worst Judging. I am now accepting nominees!”

The complaint points to the more than 402 threats made against individual federal judges this fiscal year, according to the U.S. Marshals Service.

The lawyer groups and former judges want the Florida Bar to discipline Percival for violating a rule prohibiting lawyers from making false statements “or with reckless disregard as to its truth or falsity concerning the qualifications or integrity of a judge.”

“Mr. Percival’s statements go far beyond normal criticism,” the complaint states. “They are unfounded ad hominem attacks that directly impugn the integrity of four sitting judges.”

Only about 25% of complaints result in the opening of a disciplinary file, according to the Florida Bar website.

Last year, the Florida Bar and the Florida Supreme Court declined to investigate an ethics complaint against former Attorney General Pam Bondi because she was a “sitting officer appointed under the U.S. Constitution.”

Before becoming DHS’s general counsel, Percival worked as then-Florida Attorney General Ashley Moody’s chief of staff and senior counsel for the Justice Department. He attended the University of Virginia School of Law.
