entries.title: Atlanta Lashes Out Over DNC’s 2028 Convention Snub
entries.summary: The city’s mayor launched a new round of criticism toward embattled DNC Chair Ken Martin.
entries.content:
Local leaders in Atlanta heavily criticized the Democratic National Committee on Thursday for rejecting the city’s bid to host the 2028 convention, accusing the national party of “abandoning” both the South and Black voters writ large.

In a letter obtained by multiple outlets, Andre Dickens, the mayor of Atlanta, blasted the DNC and its embattled chair, Ken Martin, for skipping over Atlanta after the committee whittled its list of finalists down to three cities: Boston, Denver and Philadelphia. Atlanta has not hosted a convention in nearly four decades.

Dickens argued that leaving out Atlanta signals the DNC and Martin are overlooking how vital the South is to the Democratic base. It is the latest criticism of Martin, who has faced pressure to step down over the party’s financial problems and internal clashes.

“They are afraid to leave their comfort zone and blind to the fact that the South is the answer,” Dickens said. “They are abandoning Atlanta, abandoning the South, and once again abandoning Black voters.”

Dickens claimed that while the Republican National Committee has chosen the South for its conventions — the most recent examples being a pared-down 2020 convention in Charlotte, North Carolina, and a 2012 gathering in Florida — the Democratic Party has instead “chosen the same region over and over again.”

“This isn’t by accident,” Dickens said. “It’s an intentional choice.”

He did not reference the 2012 Democratic convention, which was also held in Charlotte.

Georgia state Rep. Ruwa Romman said the Democrats cannot achieve a “path to power without the South.”

“Party people keep saying black voters and black women are the base of the party yet don't bother to invest in the region with the largest concentration of black voters,” Romman, a Democrat, wrote in a post on X.

Atlanta launched a vigorous campaign to woo the DNC after losing the 2024 convention to Chicago. Atlanta City Council members approved up to $36 million earlier in August to host the event and had secured a contract with the Metropolitan Atlanta Rapid Transit Authority for transportation.

Dickens spokesperson Michael Smith told The Atlanta-Journal Constitution that it was “unfortunate” to learn about the DNC’s decision through news reports and that the mayor’s office would have “more to say on this in the future.”

Martin said in a statement that the three finalists presented “incredibly strong bids to host the convention.”

The DNC did not elaborate Thursday on why it cut Atlanta and Chicago from the running. It did not immediately reply to a request for comment on Dickens’ letter or Smith’s claims.

Martin wrote on X that each city “presented strong bids to host an inspiring celebration of our party’s future nominee and a critical step on our path to retaking the White House.”

Site visits to all five locations were conducted in April and May. Factors that played into the decision-making process included a city’s operational and logistical capacity, shared Democratic values and ability to respond to the challenges that arise from hosting the convention, according to a DNC official.

The DNC chose South Carolina as the first state in the party’s 2028 presidential primary process — a move that party strategists and leaders said would challenge candidates to earn the votes of Black and Latino constituents early on in the process. The party is also providing an additional $5,000 per month to Republican-controlled states, including nine Southern states, to support Democratic candidates.

entries.title: Trump Administration Demands Release of U.S. Citizen ‘Wrongfully’ Detained in China
entries.summary: Min Zin, a U.S. citizen who was working in Myanmar, was detained.
entries.content:
The State Department has called for the immediate release of a U.S. citizen arrested in China on spying charges — a detainment that the department declared “wrongful” on Thursday.

Min Zin is a U.S. scholar who was working in Myanmar and leading a think tank focused on the country. Zin’s research focuses on democratization, and he was a student activist in 1988 during Myanmar’s pro-democracy movement.

In June, he traveled to Yunnan province in China, which borders Myanmar, for an academic conference. He was invited by the Chinese government.

In a press release, the State Department said there are now two U.S. citizens who have been “wrongfully detained” in China: Zin and Dr. Youlin Chen. Chen, who is from Boston, has been detained for two years without trial, according to his family. He was declared a wrongful detainee in March by the State Department, and in May, Trump brought up Chen’s case to Chinese leader Xi Jinping, but nothing was resolved. Chen was a U.S. seismologist tracking nuclear tests who was also detained on espionage charges.

“The safety and security of U.S. citizens is the State Department’s top priority. We will continue to advocate for Mr. Zin and call for the release of all U.S. citizens who are arbitrarily detained or exit banned in China,” the department said in the release.

China’s foreign ministry confirmed early Friday that Zin had been arrested, as he was suspected of spying and endangering Chinese national security.

The Chinese Embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Institute for Strategy and Policy-Myanmar, which Min helped found, said it welcomes the State Department’s designation of Min’s detainment as wrongful.

“We humbly ask that the US government continues to keep Min Zin’s case as a top priority, particularly ahead of President Xi’s visit to meet with President Trump next month, and that the People’s Republic of China (PRC) facilitate his immediate and unconditional release,” the institute said in a statement. “We sincerely hope he can reunite with his family and team soon.”

President Donald Trump is set to meet with Xi in D.C. on Sept. 24 — the second meeting in four months between the two. They met in Beijing in May.

entries.title: Democrat Aisha Wahab Wins Special Election to Replace Eric Swalwell
entries.summary: Wahab defeated Melissa Hernandez in the special election and will face her again in the November midterms
entries.content:
Democrat Aisha Wahab has won the special election to serve the rest of former Rep. Eric Swalwell’s House term.

The Associated Press called the race Thursday evening.

Wahab defeated Bay Area Rapid Transit Board President Melissa Hernandez, also a Democrat, on Thursday. The pair will face off again in November. California holds jungle primaries, in which the top two candidates advance to the general election regardless of political affiliation.

Wahab, the first Afghan American to serve in Congress, is a progressive Democrat and served in the California state Senate. Her campaign focused on affordable housing, protecting Medicare, banning congressional stock trading and supporting small businesses.

Swalwell, who was once a leading contender in the California governor’s race, dropped out of the race and resigned from Congress amid sexual assault allegations, which he denies.
